$schema-note: SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH for every hard-coded port in the two test families that
bind real sockets on a developer/CI machine:
(a) `harnesses` — the six live e2e gates under e2e/local/run-*.sh. Consumed by
e2e/local/lib/harness.sh (`harness_ports <name>`), which exports each key
as a shell variable of the same name.
(b) `vitest`    — root-sweep suites with intentionally hard-coded listeners.
Real nats-server suites use atomic OS-assigned ports and are still scanned
by e2e/local/ports.test.ts so a reintroduced fixed port fails the guard.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS (#118, #119): these two families used to pick ports
independently. When they overlapped, nats-server could not bind and the suite
died in beforeAll — or worse, a gate silently exercised nothing. Two real
collisions were shipped this way:
* 18222 — nats-transport-realserver's monitor port vs the default NATS URL
baked into two-account-isolation-roundtrip.ts.
* 3981  — run-turn-outcome.sh and run-derived-trust.sh both claimed it.
RULES:
1. Every hard-coded port under `harnesses` and `vitest` must be globally unique. Two
harnesses may NOT share a port even if they never run concurrently today:
that assumption is what #119 was. e2e/local/ports.test.ts enforces this.
2. Nothing may claim a port listed in `reserved`.
3. Adding a port means editing THIS file. Two branches adding ports collide
here as a merge conflict — which is the point. A collision must never be
discoverable only as a flaky `nats-server did not become ready`.
4. Do not re-introduce a hard-coded port default in a driver. The gate passes
every port via env; drivers must fail loudly on a missing env var rather
than fall back to a literal that silently drifts out of sync (that drift
is exactly how the 18222 collision survived).

$note: ECHO_PORT was 18907 — the same port run-two-account-isolation.sh uses for
its account-B echo server. ISSUER_PORT was 3981 — the same port
run-turn-outcome.sh uses (#119). Both were moved here, not there: the other
two harnesses' values sit inside coherent per-harness blocks (…06/…07 as an
A/B pair; the …81 family), so this harness was the interloper in each case.
Root-sweep suites that intentionally hard-code real socket listeners. They
run on every `npm test`, so they contend with the gate family for ports
exactly like another gate would. Suites whose server atomically requests
OS-assigned ports do not allocate entries here.
Also a root-sweep suite that binds real sockets, so it belongs under the
same authority. It spawns `nats-server -p 4222 -js` (binding 0.0.0.0:4222,
not loopback) plus two HTTP servers. 4222 was previously listed under
`reserved` as merely 'a dev server may hold it' — that was wrong: this
repo claims it on every `npm test`.
The ports are declared here so ports.test.ts enforces them like any other
allocation. The suite still hard-codes its own literals; wiring it to read
this file is deliberately NOT done here, because that suite has separate
defects under review (its skip guard does not fire on a dead child, and
Test 10 never connects to NATS at all).
Non-suite files that legitimately hard-code a port of their own. They are
declared owners: the literal in the file IS the allocation, so ports.test.ts
allows exactly these numbers in exactly these files and nothing else.
Ports nothing in this repo's test families may claim, with the reason. These
are not allocations — they are exclusions.
reserved.3951: a developer's live SaaS issuer, by local convention
reserved.3961: a developer's live SaaS base URL, by local convention
reserved.8080: stock dev HTTP port — a dev server may hold it
